intro: “Thoreau” is the fourth movement of Ives’s Piano Sonata No. 2, “Concord, Mass., 1840–60”, and depicts a walk around Walden Pond. After a restless passage the music settles over a repeated A–C–G in the bass, and the Concord Sonata ends on high chords.

sections.label: Intro · Rising chords in two keys
sections.mNote: Quiet piano figures rise through the opening.

sections.label: A · Three walks from G major
sections.mNote: Each walk begins, quickens and subsides.

sections.label: B · A–C–G repeated in the bass
sections.mNote: A freer melody moves above the repeated notes.

sections.label: C · Repeated dissonant piano chords
sections.mNote: Dissonant piano chords build to a sustained climax.

sections.label: D · Bass figure A–C–G returns
sections.mNote: A–C–G returns before the opening figures are heard again.

sections.label: E · Sonata melody returns
sections.mNote: The recurring tune sounds above repeated piano figures.

sections.label: Coda · High chords over lower echo
sections.mNote: High chords sound above an earlier phrase in the bass.

cues.title: Opening chords in two keys
cues.text: Rising chords in the piano sound in two keys at once. Their small upward steps return near the end of the movement.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, “Thoreau”: rising opening figures and chords in two keys, later recalled. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ives’s 1920 essay on Thoreau
cues.text: In his 1920 essay Ives placed Thoreau beside Walden Pond on an autumn day, “a shadow of a thought at first, colored by the mist and haze over the pond”. In his account the mist lifts, and Thoreau grows restless and starts walking.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Thoreau”, paragraph beginning “And if there shall be a program”. Quotation retains Ives’s American spelling. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#thoreau

cues.title: Three walking episodes
cues.text: A plain G major chord begins the first of three walking episodes. Each one quickens and grows louder, then falls back. The last builds to a bell-like climax.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the three G major beginnings, accelerating walks and final bell-like climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Thoreau’s walks in the Essays
cues.text: In Ives’s imagined day Thoreau walks the white-pebbled eastern shore, the “bolder northern” and western shores, and the railroad track “where the Aeolian harp plays”. Each quicker stride is still short of the “tempo of Nature”. Ives wrote that Thoreau’s freedom lay “in his submission to her”.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Thoreau”, the paragraph beginning “And if there shall be a program”: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#thoreau. Gann matches the three walks to the three G major episodes: https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: A–C–G ostinato in the bass
cues.text: A–C–G rises repeatedly in the bass as an ostinato. Above it the piano plays an independent melody in another key.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the A–C–G ostinato after the walks and the independent upper melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Concord bell
cues.text: In Ives’s account, the evening is interrupted only by “the faint sound of the Concord bell”, because it is prayer-meeting night in the village. Kyle Gann hears the bell in a series of soft, dissonant chords, after which the music moves towards its climax.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Thoreau”: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#thoreau. Gann, “Thoreau”, on the images that lead to the climax: https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repeated chords and climax
cues.text: The piano repeats chords that grow more dissonant. Earlier in this passage a dotted-rhythm figure appears that is related to the sonata’s recurring melody. The repetition leads to a climax.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: dotted-rhythm figure related to the human-faith melody and the ensuing repetitive, dissonant climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performance for Max Smith, 1912
cues.text: In a memo of 1913 Ives noted that the year before he had played the Concord Sonata for his friend Max Smith, a music critic, with Thoreau still rather improvised.
cues.evidence: Gann’s timeline of the sonata, 1912 entry, citing Ives’s 1913 memo: https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Return of the A–C–G ostinato
cues.text: Converging chords follow the climax. The A–C–G ostinato and its melody return, and then figures from the opening page come back.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: converging chords after the climax, return of the ostinato and melody, then introductory figures. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ives on Thoreau, 1920
cues.text: Thoreau played the flute, though Ives was more interested in his ear. In the opening paragraph of “Thoreau” in Essays Before a Sonata (1920), Ives wrote that Thoreau “did not have to go to Boston to hear ‘the Symphony’”.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), opening paragraph of “Thoreau”. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#thoreau

cues.title: Return of the cyclic melody
cues.text: The sonata’s recurring melody returns above repeating figures from the movement’s opening. Later the A–C–G ostinato takes over beneath it. The same tune was heard at length in The Alcotts; here it returns in a much quieter ending.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: cyclic melody over introductory figures, then the ostinato. Ives supplies a piano-only alternative to the flute version; this recording credits piano alone. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Flute sketch, 1911
cues.text: In Ives’s evening, “the poet’s flute is heard out over the pond”. A sketch with a flute playing the sonata’s main melody probably dates from 1911, when Ives holidayed at Pell’s in the Adirondacks and conceived the sonata. The sketch does not yet contain the Beethoven motive.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Thoreau”: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#thoreau. Gann’s timeline, 1911 entry: https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Closing bars, high chords
cues.text: The opening figures return briefly, followed by chords high on the piano. An earlier phrase sounds beneath them. The final notes keep a slight dissonance, unlike the plain C major ending of The Alcotts.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”, final paragraph: introductory recollection, high chords and lower earlier motive, ending with slight dissonance. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: G major chord opens first walking episode
transitions.from: Intro · Rising chords in two keys
transitions.to: A · Three walks from G major
transitions.how: The rising piano figures lead to a plain G major chord, which begins the first of three walking episodes. Each episode grows quicker and louder before falling back, and the same G major chord begins the second and third.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the introduction and the three walking episodes with G major beginnings. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: A–C–G ostinato in the bass
transitions.from: A · Three walks from G major
transitions.to: B · A–C–G repeated in the bass
transitions.how: The last walk reaches a bell-like climax. The piano then begins repeating A–C–G in the bass, and a melody in another key moves freely above it. The left hand keeps returning to the same three notes while the right hand plays an independent line.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the end of the walks, A–C–G ostinato and independent upper melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Dotted rhythms lead to repeated chords
transitions.from: B · A–C–G repeated in the bass
transitions.how: The piano writing becomes more animated, with a dotted-rhythm figure related to the sonata’s recurring melody. Repeated dissonant chords then build to a climax.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the animated dotted-rhythm passage and later repetitive, dissonant climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Converging chords and the returning bass figure
transitions.how: The dissonant climax subsides in converging chords in the piano. The A–C–G figure returns in the bass, below the wandering melody heard earlier. Figures from the opening page then interrupt the bass figure and the melody, and they gradually become more agitated.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: converging chords, return of the ostinato and melody, followed by the introductory figures. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Recurring melody over the introductory figures
transitions.how: The sonata’s recurring melody enters above repeating figures from the introduction. As the melody continues, the accompaniment changes to the A–C–G ostinato, so the same tune runs over both piano patterns.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”: the cyclic melody over introductory figures and then the ostinato, with flute and piano-only versions. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: High chords above an earlier phrase
transitions.to: Coda · High chords over lower echo
transitions.how: The recurring melody drops out and the piano’s ostinato continues alone. The opening figures return briefly. The piano then plays high chords, with an earlier phrase in the lower register beneath them. The last notes keep a slight dissonance.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Thoreau”, final paragraph: ostinato, introductory recollection, high chords and lower motive. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

composer.epithet: Composer and New York life-insurance salesman whose music sets a hymn heard across a river against a marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut, where his son Charles was born in 1874.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, a set of variations for keyboard on the tune of God Save the King. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and the construction of a symphony. His First Symphony, written in a European idiom, came out of that teaching. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term.
